extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, and judges (United Kingdom practice, historical Acts 1883/1888)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for conducting and defending actions for patent infringement in UK courts, covering evidence, judge/jury functions, remedies (damages, account of profits, injunctions, delivery/destruction), costs and certificates, and actions to restrain threatening conduct by patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court distrust of experiments made to manufacture evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court looks with distrust on experiments conducted for the express purpose of manufacturing evidence for the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Young v. Fernie; Betts v. Neilson. Use caution with evidence of experiments done solely to create proof for litigation; such experiments will be viewed skeptically by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on admitting evidence beyond delivered particulars (s.29(4), Act of 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 4th subsection of the 29th section of the Act of 1883, no evidence is to be admitted at the hearing except by leave of the Court or a judge in proof of any alleged infringement or objection of which particulars have not been delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court has discretionary power to allow evidence to go beyond the particulars of breaches or objections (Britain v. Hirsch). Examples where evidence beyond particulars was admitted: sales to a third person when defendant admitted transactions with him (Sykes v. Howarth). Parties should seek leave before attempting to introduce evidence outside delivered particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onus of proof for lack of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: In actions for infringement the onus of proof with regard to want of novelty is on the defendant, and therefore in an uncontested case the plaintiff is not bound to prove the novelty of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peroni v. Hudson. Defendants bear burden to prove anticipation or prior art; plaintiffs need not proactively prove novelty unless contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers to supply generic products not evidence of intent to infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer to execute orders for a class of articles (when no particular form is mentioned) is not evidence of an intention to infringe a patent for that class where the specification does not claim every kind of that class of article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where specification does not claim every kind, it is presumed that offers refer to non-infringing forms (Grainne v. Drysdale). Be specific in offers/advertising to avoid inference of intent to infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and limits of expert/scientific witness opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion of scientific witnesses is only admissible as proof of facts; their opinion whether there has been an infringement or not is, strictly speaking, inadmissible, and if objected to ought to be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific witnesses may be asked in an ordinary way what they understand by the specification (per Lord Halsbury in Kayce v. Chubb). Experts can elucidate technical facts but construction of law/specification and ultimate infringement are for the Court/jury as legal/factual determinations (cases cited: Bodington?; Lancashire & Yorkshire Railway Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge duty to explain specification to jury
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent case is tried before a jury it is the duty of the judge, where a specification comes into question, to explain to the jury what that instrument directs to be done, and it is for the jury to say whether, upon the evidence, the promised result will be accomplished by pursuing those directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Cresswell, J., Beard v. Egerton. Judge interprets directions; jury evaluates evidence on whether carrying them out achieves the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of specification is for the Court; attendant technical meaning may be for jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of a specification belongs to the Court alone, but if the case is tried before a jury, attendant circumstances and the true meaning of technical phrases are questions to be ascertained by the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Neilson v. Harford; Bovill v. Pimm; United Telephone Co. v. Bassano. If novelty or infringement depends merely on construction, it's a question of law for the judge; where imitation/ resemblance of machines involves factual comparison it becomes mixed law and fact for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: When identity of inventions from contemporaneous specifications is for Court vs jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Where identity of inventions described in two nearly contemporaneous specifications can be determined by a simple comparison of the specifications, the question is for the Court; if more than simple comparison is required, it must be submitted to the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Coltman, J., Allen v. Rawson; per other authorities. If language is plain and meaning clear, judge decides; conflicting evidence or need for expert interpretation points to jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement is mixed question of law and fact; judge will take case away if no evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of infringement is one of mixed law and fact. The judge may and ought to say there is no evidence to go to the jury if the plaintiff has offered no evidence to prove infringement; but if evidence tends to show use of substantially the same means to obtain the same result, and experts attest such use, it becomes a jury question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Lord Campbell in De la Rue v. Dickinson. Judge assesses sufficiency of plaintiff's evidence to go to the jury (see also general principle from House of Lords cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must elect between damages and account of profits
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff in a patent action cannot have both damages and an account of profits, but must elect which he will adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: (AV? v. Hett?). Plaintiffs should choose remedy strategy; rules and precedents govern available relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of damages: every unlicensed sale presumed damage to patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sale without licence of a patent article must be a damage to the patentee, and inquiry in a patent case will extend to the sale by the defendant of any articles made by him since the infringement was commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darport v. Rylands and subsequent authorities. The inquiry covers sales within six years before proceedings commenced; where plaintiff is an assignee, computation starts from registration of assignment (Elm? v. Christy). Defendant must file an affidavit stating numbers sold and purchasers' names/addresses when account taken (Murray v. Clayton; American Braided Wire Co. v. Thomson). The account may be taken notwithstanding an appeal (Saxby v. Easterbrook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate remedies against manufacturer and user
rubrics_metrics.description: Where separate proceedings have been taken against the manufacturer and user of the patented article, the plaintiff may have an account of profits against the manufacturer and damages against the user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penn v. Bibby; United Telephone Co. v. Walker. Remedies can be allocated across defendants depending on their roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on claiming both manufacturing profit and ordinary royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who is himself a manufacturer and who habitually licensed the use of his invention for a fixed royalty is not entitled to claim as against an infringer a manufacturing profit in addition to his ordinary royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penn v. Jack. Historical licensing practices may limit available remedies against infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay can bar account of profits prior to bill filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there has been unnecessary delay in filing the bill an account of profits before the filing of the bill will not be ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited: Harrison v. Taylor; Beard v. Turner; Ford v. Foster; Crossley v. Derby Gas Light Co. Plaintiffs should act promptly to preserve right to pre-bill account of profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff entitled to know defendant's prior profits when estimating account of profits
rubrics_metrics.description: In taking the account of profits made by the use of his invention, a successful plaintiff is entitled to know for comparison the profits made by the defendants in their business prior to the date at which they first used the plaintiff's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Siddett v. Vickers. Historical profit figures of defendant are relevant to apportioning profits attributable to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of damages focuses on patentee's actual loss, not infringer's profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The material question in estimating damages is the actual loss entailed on the patentee, not the profit made by the infringer; measure is the extent to which infringing articles interfered with the sale of the patented goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United Horseshoe Company v. Stewart and other authorities. Assessment should center on lost sales/market displacement rather than defendant's gross profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of allowed amendment (disclaimer/compromise/explanation) on damages (Patents Act 1888 s.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an amendment by way of disclaimer, correction, or explanation has been allowed under the Patents Act of 1888 (sect. 20), no damages are obtainable in any action in respect of the use of the invention before the amendment unless the patentee establishes to the satisfaction of the Court that his original claim was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments narrowing claims can limit retrospective damages unless good-faith drafting is proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may refuse damages for infringements occurring when patent lapsed for non-payment (Patents Act 1888 s.77(4b) style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act directs that if any proceeding shall be in respect of an infringement of a patent committed after failure to make any prescribed payment within the prescribed time and before enlargement of the time, the Court before which the proceeding is proposed may, if it thinks fit, refuse to award any damages in respect of such infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to keep payments prescribed by statute (renewals/fees) may deprive the plaintiff of damages for the period of default; discretion lies with the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to perpetual injunction when validity and infringement proved
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff is entitled to a perpetual injunction to restrain future infringements when the validity of the patent has been conclusively established, and the fact of infringement has been proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant submits, injunction may be obtained without trial. Rule 16 of Order LVIII S.C.R. provides limited stays pending appeal; injunctions may be subject to appellate orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee who disclaims cannot enforce earlier injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee after disclaiming will not be allowed to enforce an injunction obtained before disclaiming, but must proceed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dudgeon v. Thomson. Amendment/disclaimer affects previously obtained remedies; fresh proceedings may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to order delivery up or destruction of infringing machines/articles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has power to order the infringing machines to be delivered up to the plaintiff, as well as any articles in the defendant's possession made by them, and may also order destruction of machines made in violation of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Betts v. De Vitre; Tangye v. Stott. However where patent is for a combination and parts can be used for other lawful purposes, the Court may refuse destruction and instead mark or render unfit for future infringing use (Needham v. Oxley; Plimpton v. Malcolmson; Frearson v. Loe). Orders can be tailored to avoid unnecessarily destroying legitimately usable parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional and procedural variances for Scotland, Ireland, Isle of Man
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act (various sections) preserves local court jurisdictions: in Scotland actions for infringement apply provisions about assessors and are tried without a jury unless otherwise directed; in Ireland parties have remedies as if the patent extended to Ireland only; Isle of Man provisions preserve local court processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 107–112 and related rules define meanings of 'the Court' and 'Court of Appeal' regionally. R.S.C. O. XL r.2: where leave to serve writ is asked in Scotland or Ireland and concurrent remedy may exist, court/judge must consider comparative cost and convenience of proceeding in England or in place of defendant's residence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to costs and higher scale in patent actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful plaintiff is entitled to his costs unless his conduct warrants deprivation; in patent actions costs are usually allowed on the higher scale because of importance, special nature and difficulty; costs as between solicitor and client are obtainable under s.31 of the Act of 1883.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff will not be deprived of costs because he didn't apply to the defendant before proceedings, or because the defendant was unaware or had no intention to do wrong (cases cited). Taxation of costs must consider particulars delivered by parties; particulars not certified as proven or reasonable/proper are not allowable on taxation (s.29(6) of Act of 1883). Counsel should apply promptly after judgment for certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates affecting costs and later actions (s.31 Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under s.31 of the Act of 1883 the Court or a judge may certify that the validity of the patent came in question; if so, in any subsequent action for infringement the plaintiff on obtaining a final order or judgment in his favour shall have full costs as between solicitor and client unless the Court/judge trying the later action certifies otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances and limits: certificate typically applies when validity was in question in a contested case; it may not be available if given after a later action was commenced (Automatic Weighing Machine Co. v. International Hygienic Society). The Vice-Chancellor of the County Palatine is not competent to grant such a certificate (Proctor v. Sutton Lodge Chemical Co.). Historic case law elaborates when certificates should be given; counsel should be aware of procedural timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation and taxation of costs for multiple/piecemeal claims and abandoned issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiffs sue on multiple patents but abandon some at trial, they must pay costs occasioned by including abandoned patents; likewise where separate suits are brought on separate patents against same defendant, costs may be limited to what would have been allowed had patents been joined. If a party succeeds on a distinct issue though defeated generally, they may recover costs of that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Imji v. Fraser; Edison v. Newcastle; United Telephone Co. v. Sharpies; Hank v. Eastman. Plaintiffs and defendants should consolidate claims or be prepared for apportionment of costs; raising issues later abandoned can shift costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs consequences when issues raised and abandoned by defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: If a defendant raises issues which are abandoned at the trial, the unsuccessful plaintiff is entitled to the costs of those issues; where a defendant contested validity but infringement proved and patent found invalid, plaintiff entitled to costs of infringement issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American Braided Wire Co. v. Thomson; Pool v. ???. Parties should consider tactical risk of raising multiple issues which, if abandoned, may shift costs adversely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third parties appearing may be ordered to pay costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties who appeared in the Court below and in the Court of Appeal, although not made defendants, were ordered to pay costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edison & Swan Co. v. Holland. Third parties entering appearances risk costs liability if involvement proves unhelpful to their position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates of proof of particulars and objections for taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: On taxation of costs regard shall be had to particulars delivered by the plaintiff and defendant, and they shall not be allowed costs in respect of particulars delivered unless certified by the Court or a judge to have been proven or to have been reasonable and proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sixth subsection of s.29 Act 1883. The taxing master has no power without the judge's certificate to allow costs of particulars of objection which the defendant had not been called to prove if action was dismissed on ground patent not subject-matter. See authorities (various cases cited). Counsel should obtain appropriate certificates to secure costs for particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory protection against threatening conduct by patentees (s.32 Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person claiming to be the patentee, by circulars, advertisements, or otherwise, threatens any other person with legal proceedings or liability in respect of any alleged manufacture, use, sale, or purchase of the invention, any person aggrieved may bring an action and obtain an injunction against continuance of such threats and recover damages if the alleged activity was not in fact an infringement of any legal rights of the person making such threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section does not apply if the person making threats, with due diligence, commences and prosecutes an action for infringement. Use the provision to restrain frivolous or coercive threats; collect evidence of communications (circulars, ads) and proof that subject activity was non-infringing.
